title: the DSG Deepearth areas 1-3

banner.title: THE DSG DEEPEARTH AREAS 1-3, R534: printed pp. 78-79 (pdf 79-80) - the individual area key opens with the first three areas: Area 1 The Great Lake (the fresh cold water fed by rapid streams and meandering rivers; the rocky mountainous northern shore with the 1,200-ft maximum depth; the sandy eastern and western shores with their fishing villages, natural harbors and 400-ft average depth; the southern limestone cliff rising 400 ft and never below 100, plunging into the water with no settlements, the 50-ft depth sloping to 400 toward the center; the 50-by-120-mile oval on limestone bedrock under silt; the trout and salmon, the carnivores and the boat-swallowing giant gars; the lonely sirines of the rugged shores and the scrags near the lake-bottom center; the fish and mill-wheel resources; and the unique features - the 20-ft half-water cave to Area 5, the water-filled northern mine shafts, and the wall-of-force-with-permanence spur corridor), Area 2 Surface Lands (the temperate terrain sloping upward south to north - farmlands, hills, mountains; the harsh winters and heavy rainfall; the fortified river-bank trading city; the centaurs, halflings, and the rumored enchanted woods of elves, pixies and dryads; the hill dwarves and hill giants at odds; the smoldering volcanoes rumored prowled by dragons; the farm-and-lumber-and-fish resources with the hill-dwarf gold, silver, copper, bloodstone and ruby sales; and the unique features - the city dungeon linking sewers to the palace dungeon and to Area 9, the thieves-guild and merchant connections, the four-level bandit dungeon with its secret passage to Area 4, the half-connecting hill caves to Area 3, and the taboo abandoned mine shaft), and Area 3 Upper Caverns (the central living-cave limestone maze with plentiful water, the 6-to-8-ft pools, the 300-ft-square excavation cap, the 20x10x100-ft largest chamber with its 3x2-ft pinches, the wall-of-force watery wall toward the lake; the raiding races - troglodytes, goblins, hobgoblins, ogres, trolls and lycanthropes - centered in their excavated dungeons; the scavengers, the gibbering mouther, greater basilisk and shambling mound, and the wandering beholder given a wide berth; the air-water-plants resources; and the unique features - the 80-ft troglodyte amphitheater with the fungus-covered war-hero statue and its 10,000-gp eye-diamonds, and the 3x1-ft magic pool with its pint-per-year drip, the 60-ft infravision, the 2d6-week durations and the 30 pints)
banner.provenance: the DSG scan (archive.org item advanced-dungeons-dragons-1st-edition), pdf = printed + 1; the text read from the IA djvu OCR (djvu.txt lines ~9840-9960) with the pdf Acrobat-Capture layer as the second read (idx 182-184 = the printed pp. 78-80 windows); the compiled-tables appendix has no reprint of this prose. A CLEAN-READ ROUND: both machine reads agree on every load-bearing number - the 1,200-ft depth, the 400-ft averages, the 50/100/400-ft cliff bands, the 50-by-120-mile oval, the 20-ft cave, the four-level dungeon, the 6-to-8-ft pools, the 300-ft cap, the 20x10x100 chamber with the 3x2 pinches, the 80-ft amphitheater, the 10,000-gp diamonds, and the magic-pool numbers (the 3x1-ft size, the pint-per-year drip, the 60-ft range, the 2d6 weeks, the 30 pints); the only garbles are the standing glyph classes (the djvu "INDIVIDGAL" and "GPPER" header noise, non-load-bearing). SEAMS: the R518 water travel (the lake navigation), the Monster Manual denizens (the scrags, sirines, beholder and the rest), the PHB wall of force and permanence spells, the R521-R522 mining (the mine shafts), and the R503 re-grain. A ZERO-FLIP ROUND: the pp. 75-98 Deepearth child remains open until the setting lands in full (the R527/R533 precedent - the gap report is NOT in the git add). Nothing auto-credits.
banner.sentinel: A procedural-plus-prose round: no tables pin. The numbers pin as consts per the R508 convention - the Great Lake depths and dimensions, the surface-lands dungeon levels, and the Upper Caverns geography and magic-pool numbers. The geography, denizens, resources and unique-features prose pins as bools for all three areas. The R518/MM/PHB/R521-R522/R503 seams are noted; the Deepearth child stays open; nothing auto-credits.

consts.name: dnarLakeMaxDepthFt
consts.comment: the Great Lake is deepest just off the rocky, mountainous northern shore, reaching a maximum depth of some 1,200 feet.

consts.name: dnarLakeAvgDepthFt
consts.comment: the average depth of the lake along the sandy eastern and western shores is about 400 feet.

consts.name: dnarLakeCliffMaxFt
consts.comment: the towering limestone cliff along the southern shore rises as much as 400 feet above the lake in places.

consts.name: dnarLakeCliffMinFt
consts.comment: the southern escarpment never drops to less than 100 feet above the water level, plunging right into the water - no settlements or beaches there.

consts.name: dnarLakeSouthDepthFt
consts.comment: the water depth at the southern cliff is usually at least 50 feet, sloping gradually to about 400 feet toward the center of the lake.

consts.name: dnarLakeWideMiles
consts.comment: the roughly oval Great Lake is about 50 miles wide; the entire lake is not shown on the map.

consts.name: dnarLakeLongMiles
consts.comment: the Great Lake is 120 miles long, its bottom resting on firm limestone bedrock covered with several feet of accumulated silt.

consts.name: dnarLakeCaveHtFt
consts.comment: the cave in the southern limestone cliffs is about 20 feet high and equally wide, only half filled with water, a gentle current leading into the depths of the earth toward Area 5.

consts.name: dnarBanditDungeonLevels
consts.comment: the bandit dungeon in the forests has four levels, several treasure caches, and many horrible monsters; a secret passage in the lowest level leads to the Area 4 cavern complex.

consts.name: dnarUpperPoolDeepLowFt
consts.comment: in the Upper Caverns none of the living caves are totally filled with water, though occasional pools are six to eight feet deep.

consts.name: dnarUpperPoolDeepHighFt
consts.comment: the upper bound of the occasional-pool depth range in the Upper Caverns.

consts.name: dnarUpperExcavatedMaxFt
consts.comment: several locations in the Upper Caverns hold dungeons excavated from the caves, though none of the excavated areas is larger than 300 feet square.

consts.name: dnarUpperChamberWidFt
consts.comment: the largest chamber in the whole Upper Caverns area is not more than 20 feet wide.

consts.name: dnarUpperChamberHtFt
consts.comment: the largest chamber is 10 feet high.

consts.name: dnarUpperChamberLongFt
consts.comment: the largest chamber is 100 feet long, each end pinched off by a narrow continuation typical of the area.

consts.name: dnarUpperPinchHtFt
consts.comment: the pinch continuations of the largest chamber are about three feet high.

consts.name: dnarUpperPinchWidFt
consts.comment: the pinch continuations are about two feet wide.

consts.name: dnarAmphitheaterDiaFt
consts.comment: the troglodytes center their holdings on a large, circular amphitheater about 80 feet in diameter.

consts.name: dnarStatueDiamondGp
consts.comment: each eye of the fungus-covered statue the troglodytes worship holds a massive diamond worth 10,000 gp, completely covered by the spreading fungus.

consts.name: dnarPoolWidFt
consts.comment: the magic pool is only three feet wide.

consts.name: dnarPoolDeepFt
consts.comment: the magic pool is one foot deep.

consts.name: dnarPoolDripPintsPerYear
consts.comment: water drips slowly into the magic pool from a stalactite at the rate of one pint per year, gaining an enchantment during the process - becoming a potion of infravision.

consts.name: dnarPoolInfraRangeFt
consts.comment: a character without infravision who drinks a pint of the magic pool water gains the ability with a 60-foot range.

consts.name: dnarPoolInfraWeeksDice
consts.comment: the infravision gained or lost from the magic pool lasts 2d6 weeks.

consts.name: dnarPoolInfraWeeksSides
consts.comment: the duration die of the magic-pool effect is a d6, two of them; characters with infravision who drink lose the ability for a similar time.

consts.name: dnarPoolPints
consts.comment: there are 30 pints of water in the magic pool; stored in an airtight container it keeps indefinitely.

bools.name: dnarLakeNorthRocky
bools.comment: the northern half of the Great Lake shore is rocky and mountainous; the eastern and western shores are lined with sandy beaches, occasional fishing villages, and a few good natural harbors.

bools.name: dnarLakeCarnivores
bools.comment: the lake is heavily populated with fish - most varieties of trout and freshwater salmon - and large freshwater carnivores are drawn to the plentiful food supply; the fishing villages tell common tales of giant gars capable of swallowing an entire boat.

bools.name: dnarLakeSirinesScrags
bools.comment: intelligent denizen reports tell of a few lonely sirines along the rugged north and south shores with their remote, isolated lairs, and a band of freshwater marine trolls - scrags - living near the center of the lake bottom, rarely disturbing fishermen and preferring the plentiful lake food supplies.

bools.name: dnarLakeMillWheels
bools.comment: the lake's primary resource is its plentiful fish supply; many communities also harness the water flow to turn mill wheels.

bools.name: dnarLakeMineShafts
bools.comment: several water-filled mine shafts in the mountainous northern shore lead to submerged caverns with openings on the bottom of the lake (see Area 2); and the small spur of the tunnel to Areas 3 and 4 - an excavated corridor cutting directly into the lake bottom - would flood very quickly had its excavator not blocked it with a wall of force augmented by permanence.

bools.name: dnarSurfaceTerrainFrame
bools.comment: the lands above Deepearth include all major temperate terrain types, generally sloping upward from south to north: fertile farmlands of a prosperous surface kingdom with villages, towns and a large city to the south, rough rocky hilly wilderness, and the towering crags of a high mountain range sealing off the north; harsh winters, mild springs, pleasant summers, heavy rainfall.

bools.name: dnarFortifiedCity
bools.comment: a fortified city on the river banks is the seat of government and a major trading center for cargoes transported over land and water; the towns and villages are primarily agricultural, each keyed to its own local needs, with small bands of bandits in the woods and foothills presenting little menace.

bools.name: dnarSurfaceRaces
bools.comment: besides humans, a small band of centaurs and several halfling villages live among the farmland forests; the deepest woods are rumored enchanted and populated by elves, pixies and dryads; both dwarves and hill giants live in the rocky hills, constantly at odds with raiding and vandalism but no pitched battle in many years; the mountains host hardy dwarves and many giants, and the far volcanic reaches are rumored prowled by dragons - few humans venture there, and fewer still return.

bools.name: dnarSurfaceResources
bools.comment: farming products - grain, milk, meat - are the primary income, with lumber harvested from the forests; water is plentiful with rowboats and sailboats common, the waters hosting many fish supporting the shore villages; and every once in awhile a band of dwarves comes down from the hills to sell gold, silver, copper, bloodstones and occasionally rubies - the mine locations a closely guarded secret.

bools.name: dnarCityDungeonSewers
bools.comment: at least one sprawling dungeon complex beneath the city connects with a natural cavern eventually leading to Area 9, linking the city sewer system to the palace dungeon; many catacomb passages connect with the sewers, a prominent thieves guild has excavated other connections, and certain merchants, wizards and lords have their own underground connections.

bools.name: dnarHillCavesHalfConnect
bools.comment: natural limestone caves are extremely common among the hills - some very shallow with no Deepearth connections, but about half connect together and lead the persevering explorer to Area 3, all of the passages natural in origin.

bools.name: dnarTabooMineShaft
bools.comment: the mountain dwarves created very deep shafts, often discontinued when striking water; a few watery connections are large enough for humans to pass, leading to exits on the bottom of the large lake; one abandoned shaft terminates in a dry cavern - the dwarves will not speak of the reason they stopped mining there, and use of that shaft is strictly taboo, though the cavern eventually leads to Area 3.

bools.name: dnarUpperMazeLiving
bools.comment: the Upper Caverns are the central area of a vast network of limestone caves - living caves with plentiful water, a virtual maze of twisting, winding caverns where cliffs, chasms and constricting passages are very common; the caverns entering from the hill region often lead directly in, and several longer natural tunnels lead to exits at dwarven mine shafts in the mountains.

bools.name: dnarUpperWallOfForce
bools.comment: the tunnel leading to the lake ends in a watery wall; only the permanent effects of a wall of force prevent the water from flooding much of the area.

bools.name: dnarUpperRaiders
bools.comment: with its relatively easy access to the surface, this part of Deepearth is inhabited by creatures that like to raid human settlements - each raiding band controlling a small section of caverns, usually centered in an excavated dungeon area: troglodytes, goblins, hobgoblins, ogres, trolls and lycanthropes, whose individual members fight each other at the slightest provocation while the communities coexist relatively peacefully.

bools.name: dnarUpperMonstersBeholder
bools.comment: a great number of unintelligent monsters roam the passages - giant rats, bats, carrion crawlers and other scavengers, plus potent individuals like a gibbering mouther, a greater basilisk and a shambling mound; a beholder also wanders the tunnels taking what it wants - the most powerful monster in the area, given a wide berth by all others.

bools.name: dnarUpperAirWaterPlants
bools.comment: the Upper Caverns have plentiful supplies of air and water, no evidence of any kind of mineral wealth, and a variety of underground plants - lichens, molds and fungi - providing the basic element in the food chain.

bools.name: dnarTroglodyteStatue
bools.comment: the troglodytes control the largest collection of dungeon and cavern areas, centered on the amphitheater with its large fungus-covered, vaguely humanoid statue worshipped as their deity - in fact a quite unremarkable sculpture of a human war hero, each eye holding a massive diamond completely covered by the spreading fungus.
